lessons.unit: Unit 1: Respectful relationships and staying safe online
lessons.title: Friendship, conflict and standing up to bullying
objectives: Describe the qualities of a good friend and signs of an unhealthy friendship
Use calm steps to resolve a disagreement
Explain what bullying is, including online, and how to be an upstander

keywords.def: hurting someone on purpose, again and again
a disagreement or argument
someone who safely helps when they see unkindness
someone who sees unkindness but does nothing
to let go of anger towards someone who has wronged you

starter: Bismillah. Name two qualities of a good friend.
Name one trusted adult you could talk to at school or at home.

teach.heading: What makes a good friend?
bullets: Does not force you to change
teach.note: Say bismillah. Ask pupils to give qualities of a good friend and write them up. Link to the hadith of the Prophet (peace be upon him): none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself (Bukhari and Muslim). Ask: ‘Would you like to be treated the way you treat your friends?’ Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass values of Integrity and Excellence (excellent manners, adab). Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: When friendships go wrong
bullets: Warning signs: bossing, leaving out, pressure
Secrets that make you worry are not safe
You are allowed to walk away
teach.note: Normalise falling out: even good friends disagree. Then separate a disagreement from unkindness that is repeated or controlling. Use invented examples: two friends both want to lead a group project (disagreement); one friend always tells another who they may sit with (control). Ask: ‘What is the difference?’ Reassure pupils that a secret that makes them feel worried, scared or uncomfortable should always be told to a trusted adult.

teach.heading: Solving disagreements calmly
bullets: Pause and breathe before you reply
teach.note: Teach the sentence frame with an example: ‘I felt left out when you started the game without me, because I wanted to join.’ Model a calm tone. Link to the hadith that the strong person is not the one who wins by strength but the one who controls himself when angry (Bukhari and Muslim). Ask: ‘Why is forgiving a sign of strength?’ Misconception: apologising means you were the only one at fault; it can simply mean you value the friendship.

teach.heading: What is bullying?
bullets: Words, leaving out, hitting or online messages
teach.note: Define bullying with the four ideas: on purpose, repeated, hurtful, power imbalance. Include cyberbullying: unkind messages, group chats that exclude someone, sharing embarrassing pictures. Refer to the TGA Anti-Bullying and Cyberbullying Policy. Ask: ‘Why might someone be unkind to others?’ Explain that reasons never excuse bullying. Remind pupils that they can report concerns to any member of staff.

teach.heading: Be an upstander
bullets: Do not join in or share
Qur'an 49:11: do not mock one another
teach.note: Teach safe ways to help: sit with the person, message them privately to say you care, save evidence, tell an adult. Cite plainly: Qur'an 49:11 tells believers not to ridicule one another or call each other bad names. Ask: ‘Which of these is easiest? Which takes courage?’ Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Integrity: doing the right thing even when others do not.

practice: Which are signs of a good friendship? (a) shares and listens (b) tells you who you may talk to (c) respects your ‘no’ (d) laughs at you in front of others.
Zainab and Hamza both want to be team leader. Write two sentences using ‘I feel… when… because…’ to sort it out calmly.
Bullying or a falling-out? (a) Two friends argue once about a game. (b) Three pupils leave Yusuf out of the group chat every week and send jokes about him.
independent: Write a short script (six lines) in which a pupil stands up for someone being left out of a group chat.
Create a poster: ‘Five ways to be an upstander’ with a Qur'an 49:11 reminder.
Write four sentences explaining how forgiving and apologising can repair a friendship.
exit: Describe one safe thing an upstander can do.
lessons.homework: Talk to a trusted adult about what they value most in a friend and write three sentences about what you learned.
lessons.send: SEND: give sentence frames and scenario cards with visuals. EAL: pre-teach ‘bullying’, ‘upstander’ and ‘forgive’ with images. Stretch: write advice for a younger pupil about handling an argument with a friend.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Respectful relationships and staying safe online
lessons.title: Online safety: who is on the other side of the screen?
objectives: Explain that people online may not be who they say they are
Describe how to protect personal information and manage chat and gaming
Know what to do if something online upsets or worries them

keywords.def: details that identify you, such as your address or school
a control that decides who can see what you share
someone you only know through a screen
to stop someone contacting you
to tell a trusted adult or the platform about a concern

starter: Bismillah. What does ‘Stop, Block, Tell’ mean?
Give one example of private information.

teach.heading: People online may not be who they say
bullets: Anyone can pretend to be someone else
Photos and names can be fake
Never agree to meet an online contact
Tell a trusted adult about any request
teach.note: Say bismillah. Use an invented example: a player in a game says they are 11 and loves the same football team, but they are actually an adult. Ask: ‘How could we find out whether someone is who they say?’ (we often cannot). Teach that real friends are people we know in real life and that trusted adults need to know about online friends. Stress that nobody will be in trouble for telling an adult. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Keep private information private
bullets: Full name, address, school and phone number
Passwords: never share, even with friends
Use three random words for a strong password
teach.note: Ask pupils to sort examples into ‘safe to share’ and ‘keep private’. Model a strong password idea: three random words such as ‘blue-tent-river’ rather than a birthday. Remind pupils not to use the same password everywhere. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Integrity: amanah means protecting what we are trusted with, including our own and others' information.

teach.heading: Games, chat and age ratings
bullets: Check age ratings such as PEGI
Keep chat to friends you know
Most social media is for ages 13 and over
teach.note: Explain that age ratings exist for protection. Show how voice and text chat can be limited with parental controls. Discuss in-game purchases and ‘free’ offers that are really tricks to get money or details. Ask: ‘What would you do if someone in a game chat was unkind or asked for personal details?’ (mute, block, leave, tell an adult).

teach.heading: Think before you click or share
bullets: Is it true? Is it kind?
Do not click strange links or ‘free’ offers
Ask permission before sharing a photo of someone
Qur'an 49:6: check news before you pass it on
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 49:6 teaches believers to verify news that comes from an unreliable source before acting on it. Show an invented message: ‘Click here to win a free console!’ Ask pupils to spot the warning signs (too good to be true, urgent, asks for details). Remind them that photos of others should not be shared without permission.

teach.heading: If something goes wrong
bullets: Close it, do not share it
Tell a trusted adult straight away
teach.note: Reassure pupils that anyone can see something upsetting by accident and that telling an adult is brave. Explain the steps: stop, close the screen, tell an adult, report or block in the app. Mention the CEOP Safety Centre for reporting online abuse and Childline for confidential support. Say the school Designated Safeguarding Lead will always help.

practice: True or false? (a) An online friend who knows all your favourite things must be who they say. (b) It is safe to share your school name in a public game chat. (c) Telling a trusted adult is always the right thing to do.
Which password is stronger and why? (a) Amina2014 (b) cloud-lemon-bridge
A game chat message says: ‘Add me and I'll give you free coins, just tell me your address.’ Write what you would do in three steps.
independent: Make a one-page ‘Safe online’ checklist for a younger pupil with five rules.
Write a short conversation in which a pupil refuses to share a password and explains why.
Design a safe username that does not give away any personal information and explain your choices.
exit: Name three pieces of private information.
What three steps should you take if something online worries you?
lessons.homework: Check the privacy settings on one app or game you use with a parent or carer, and write three sentences about what you changed or checked.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a sort-the-cards activity and a visual ‘Stop, Block, Tell’ prompt. EAL: use icons for key words. Stretch: write a short guide for parents on talking to children about online friends.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Change, wellbeing and healthy habits
lessons.title: Moving up: managing change, worries and resilience
objectives: Explain that change and worry are a normal part of life
Identify helpful ways to manage worries before moving to secondary school
Link sabr and trust in Allah to resilience

keywords.def: moving from one stage or place to another
a feeling of worry or unease
bouncing back and coping with difficulty
patience and steadfastness
trusting Allah after doing your best

starter: Bismillah. Name two feelings people may have when something changes.
Who could you talk to if you felt worried?

teach.heading: Change is part of life
bullets: New school, new routines, new friends
Qur'an 2:286: Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity
teach.note: Say bismillah. Ask pupils to think of changes they have already coped with, without personal stories: starting school, a new teacher, moving up a year. Normalise mixed feelings of excitement and nerves. Cite plainly: Qur'an 2:286, that Allah does not burden any soul beyond what it can bear. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Resilience. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: What worries look like
bullets: Common worries: homework, friends, getting lost
teach.note: Explain that worry affects both thoughts and the body. Ask pupils to suggest common worries about secondary school. Collect them anonymously through the question box if preferred. Reassure them that worry means they care, and that it can be managed. Point out that if worry is stopping someone from doing things they want to do, they should talk to an adult.

teach.heading: Tools for managing worry
bullets: Slow breathing: in for 4, out for 6
Make a plan or a list
teach.note: Teach and practise slow breathing together on camera. Teach ‘worry time’: write the worry down, plan one small step. Cite plainly: Qur'an 13:28, that hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Explain that du'a is a way to share our worries with Allah, alongside talking to people. Misconception: worrying more will keep you safe; planning helps more.

teach.heading: What can I control?
bullets: Cannot control: other people, the past
Do your best, then trust Allah
teach.note: Draw two circles: ‘I can control’ and ‘I cannot control’. Ask pupils to place worries in each. Cite plainly: Qur'an 94:5-6, that with hardship comes ease. Cite Qur'an 3:159: when you have decided, put your trust in Allah. Explain tawakkul as effort plus trust, not doing nothing.

teach.heading: Getting support
teach.note: Show the circle of support: family, friends, school staff, helplines. Ask: ‘Who could you ask for help and what would you say?’ Practise a sentence such as ‘I am feeling worried about… can we talk?’. Remind pupils of the pastoral team. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Resilience.

practice: Sort into ‘I can control’ or ‘I cannot control’: (a) how hard I revise (b) what the weather is (c) how I treat others (d) what other people say.
Write three things you are looking forward to about secondary school and one worry.
Practise slow breathing for one minute, then describe how you feel.
independent: Write a letter to a new Year 7 pupil giving three tips for coping with nerves.
Create a ‘worry plan’: choose one worry, list two things you can do and one person to ask.
Design a bookmark with a calming du'a or Qur'an 94:5-6 and three coping steps.
exit: Name two ways to manage a worry.
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph about a time you coped well with change (no names needed) and which strategy helped.
lessons.send: SEND: use visual breathing guides and choice boards. EAL: provide a feelings vocabulary sheet. Stretch: research how people in the Seerah showed sabr and tawakkul and write a short summary.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Change, wellbeing and healthy habits
lessons.title: Healthy habits: sleep, screens, food and movement
objectives: Explain how sleep, screen time, food and exercise affect health and mood
Plan a balanced daily routine
Link caring for the body to gratitude and the Islamic principle of moderation

keywords.def: eating a range of foods in the right amounts
time spent using a phone, tablet, computer or TV
avoiding too much or too little
good, pure and wholesome
a regular pattern of activities

starter: Bismillah. Name two foods that give you energy.
What is one healthy habit you already have?

teach.heading: Your body has a right over you
bullets: Care for it with food, sleep and activity
Hadith: your body has a right over you
Health is a blessing to be thankful for
teach.note: Say bismillah. Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said, ‘Your body has a right over you’ (Bukhari). Also mention that health and free time are two blessings many people take for granted (Bukhari). Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Contentment (shukr) and Progress. Ask: ‘How can we show thanks for our health?’ Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Sleep
bullets: Aim for about 9 to 11 hours at this age
Screens off an hour before bed
Sleep helps mood, memory and growth
teach.note: Explain that sleep is when the body and brain recover. Tired children find it hard to concentrate and may feel more irritable or worried. Suggest a wind-down routine: wudu, dhikr, reading. Ask: ‘What stops people from sleeping well?’ Mention that a good routine also helps with Fajr.

teach.heading: Screens and balance
bullets: Screens can be fun and useful
Too much can affect sleep and mood
Take breaks and look away from the screen
teach.note: Avoid blame. Discuss the difference between helpful uses (learning, connecting) and habits that take over. Teach: take a break every 30-40 minutes, keep devices out of bedrooms at night if possible, and agree family rules. Ask pupils to consider how they feel after one hour of gaming compared with one hour outdoors.

teach.heading: Food and drink
bullets: Eat fruit, vegetables, protein and starch
Qur'an 2:168: eat what is lawful and good
teach.note: Use the NHS Eatwell Guide as a model without detailed numbers. Cite plainly: Qur'an 2:168 tells people to eat of what is lawful and good. Qur'an 7:31 says to eat and drink but not to be excessive. Be sensitive about family circumstances and avoid pupils sharing what they eat at home. Teach that no food is ‘bad’; balance is the key.

teach.heading: Move, rest and keep clean
bullets: Aim for about 60 minutes of activity a day
Walking, sports, games and prayer all count
Wash regularly: cleanliness is half of faith
teach.note: State the UK Chief Medical Officers' guidance that children and young people should average at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity a day. Link to the hadith that cleanliness is half of faith (Muslim). Remind pupils that daily washing and clean clothes become more important as they grow older. Ask them to create a simple weekly plan.

practice: True or false? (a) You can catch up on all your sleep at the weekend. (b) Water is a good drink choice. (c) A short break from a screen helps your eyes.
List three things that could be part of a calm bedtime routine.
A pupil spends all of Saturday on a screen. Suggest two small changes for tomorrow.
independent: Create a one-day routine for a school day including sleep, food, activity, prayer and screen time.
Make a poster: ‘Thank Allah for your health’ with five ways to look after your body.
Write a short diary of your habits for two days and decide on one change.
exit: Give two benefits of getting enough sleep.
Name one way to balance screen time.
lessons.homework: Keep a note of your screen time and bedtime for three days and write two sentences about what you notice.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a template routine with pictures. EAL: label images of food groups and habits. Stretch: research how sleep affects learning and present three facts.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Money matters
lessons.title: Earning money
lessons.bigQuestion: Is all money earned in the same way equally good?
objectives: To understand how people earn money and why honest, halal work matters
successCriteria: All: name different ways people earn money
Most: explain how skills and training affect pay
Some: explain what makes earnings halal
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and dignity in work

keywords.def: get money for work
money paid for work, often per hour
a fixed amount paid each year, usually monthly
money earned in a way Islam allows (حَلَال)

hook.text: Is all money earned in the same way equally good?
hook.a: No: money from honest, halal work is good; money from cheating or haram work is not.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said that no one eats better food than what he earns with his own hands, and that the Prophet Dawud ate from the work of his hands (al-Bukhari). Allah says: 'disperse in the land and seek of the bounty of Allah' (al-Jumu'ah 62:10).

teach.heading: Ways to earn
teach.note: Examples: nurse, builder, shopkeeper, teacher, programmer.

teach.heading: Wages and salaries
bullets: Skills and training often raise pay
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Hassan earns £12 an hour and works 30 hours. Weekly pay?

teach.heading: Halal earnings
bullets: Not from haram goods or riba
teach.note: Sort.

cards: Selling fruit at a fair price
Hiding faults when selling a car

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

practice.q: Why might a surgeon earn more than a shop assistant?
practice.a: Years of training and specialist skills.

independent.q: Core: Job cards (pupil PDF): work out weekly pay for four jobs.
independent.a: Answers on the teacher key.

independent.q: Extend: Choose a job you might like. Write the skills and training it needs.
independent.a: A job with relevant skills.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why earning from haram sources is not allowed even if it pays more.
independent.a: Islam values honest, halal provision over profit; haram earnings harm others and bring no barakah.

exit.q: A salary is... A) paid per hour B) a fixed yearly amount paid monthly C) a gift
exit.a: B) a fixed yearly amount paid monthly
options: A fixed yearly amount paid monthly

exit.q: Big question: is all money equally good? Why?
exit.a: No: only halal, honest earnings are good.

lessons.homework: Ask a family member about their first job and what they learned.
lessons.send: SEND: multiplication grid for pay. EAL: earn, wage, salary. Stretch: work out a yearly salary from monthly pay.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Money matters
lessons.title: Value for money
lessons.bigQuestion: A big pack and a small pack of rice. Is the big pack always cheaper?
objectives: To understand how to compare prices and choose value for money
successCriteria: All: compare two prices
Most: work out unit prices to compare packs
Some: explain why the cheapest is not always best value
lessons.smsc: Moral: wise spending and avoiding waste

keywords.def: getting good quality for the price
the price for one item or one unit, such as per 100 g
look at the differences
a message trying to persuade us to buy

hook.text: A big pack and a small pack of rice. Is the big pack always cheaper?
hook.a: Not always: check the price per kilogram.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ taught that honesty blesses trade and hiding faults removes the blessing (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Buyers should think carefully and avoid waste (al-Isra 17:26-27).

starter.a: Money paid for work per hour.

teach.heading: Comparing prices
teach.note: Supermarket labels show price per kg or per 100 g.

teach.heading: Unit price
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Rice: 1 kg for £1.80 or 5 kg for £7.50. Which is better value?
steps: The 5 kg bag is better value, if you will use it

teach.heading: Not just price
bullets: Quality and how long it lasts
Will we use it all? Waste costs
teach.note: A 'buy one get one free' is only good if we need two.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Pack A: 4 for £2. Pack B: 6 for £2.40. Cheaper each?

practice.q: Juice: 1 litre £1.20 or 2 litres £2.00. Better value per litre?
practice.model: Teacher divides £2.00 by 2 = £1 per litre and compares with £1.20.

independent.q: Core: Shopping comparison sheet: find the better value for five pairs (pupil PDF).
independent.a: Answers on the teacher key.

independent.q: Extend: Explain when the bigger pack is not the best choice.
independent.a: When it would go off or not be used: waste.

independent.q: Stretch: Analyse an advert's 'offer' and decide if it is really good value.
independent.a: A reasoned judgement using unit price and need.

exit.q: Unit price means... A) the price of the shop B) price for one unit C) the biggest price
exit.a: B) price for one unit

exit.q: Big question: is the big pack always cheaper?
exit.a: Not always: compare unit prices.

lessons.homework: With a grown-up, compare unit prices of one item at home (or online) and decide the best value.
lessons.send: SEND: calculator allowed and simpler numbers. EAL: compare, value, offer. Stretch: compare three sizes.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Money matters
lessons.title: Lending, borrowing and riba
lessons.bigQuestion: Your friend lends you £10 and asks for £12 back. Is that fair?
objectives: To understand how borrowing works, why riba (interest) is forbidden in Islam and what halal alternatives exist
successCriteria: All: explain what borrowing and lending mean
Most: explain what interest is and why Islam forbids riba
Some: describe a halal alternative such as saving first or a qard hasan (interest-free loan)
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness and the harm of debt

keywords.def: take money you must pay back
give money that will be paid back
extra money charged on a loan
interest on loans, forbidden in Islam (رِبَا)
a goodly loan with no interest (قَرْض حَسَن)

hook.text: Your friend lends you £10 and asks for £12 back. Is that fair?
hook.a: In Islam, no: asking extra on a loan is riba.

islamicLink.text: Islamic note: riba (رِبَا) is forbidden (Qur'an 2:275: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba). Islamic finance uses partnership (mushārakah, مُشَارَكَة) and cost-plus sale (murābaḥah, مُرَابَحَة) instead. A Muslim may lend as a kindness (qard hasan) and should repay debts on time.

teach.heading: Borrowing and lending
bullets: Borrow: take now, pay back later
Lend: give now, get back later
teach.note: Islam treats debt seriously: repay on time.

teach.heading: What is interest?
bullets: Banks and credit cards charge it
teach.note: This is how the wider economy works; it is knowledge, not something to take.

teach.heading: Halal alternatives
bullets: Qard hasan: a loan with no extra
teach.note: Murabahah: the bank buys the item and sells it at an agreed higher price, paid in parts; no interest on money.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Borrow £200 at 10% for a year. Paid back?
check.why: 10% of £200 is £20, so £220. In Islam, this extra is riba.

practice.q: Borrow £50 at 20% for one year. Paid back?

practice.a: A loan with no interest, given as a kindness.

independent.q: Core: Scenarios sheet: for three money problems, choose a halal option and explain (pupil PDF).
independent.a: Save first; borrow from family as qard hasan; buy second-hand.

independent.q: Extend: Explain in the portal response box why riba can harm people. Start: 'Riba can harm people because...'
independent.a: Riba can harm people because debts grow, the poor pay more and wealth flows to lenders.

exit.q: Riba is... A) charity B) interest on loans, forbidden in Islam C) a type of savings
exit.a: B) interest on loans, forbidden in Islam
options: Interest on loans, forbidden in Islam

exit.q: Big question: lend £10, ask £12 back: is it fair in Islam?
exit.a: No: the extra £2 is riba.

lessons.homework: Ask a grown-up how your family saves for big things, and write one way to buy without riba.
lessons.send: SEND: worked percentage steps. EAL: borrow, lend, interest. Stretch: research one Islamic bank product (murabahah).

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Money matters
lessons.title: Achieving goals: saving for something that matters
lessons.bigQuestion: Would you rather have £5 now, or £20 in a month if you save? What helps you wait?
objectives: To understand how to plan and save towards a financial goal without debt
successCriteria: All: set a saving goal with a price
Most: work out how long it will take to save
Some: adjust the plan by cutting wants or earning a little more

keywords.def: an amount we aim to save for something
the amount we need
how long it will take
giving up something now for later

hook.text: Would you rather have £5 now, or £20 in a month if you save? What helps you wait?

islamicLink.text: Patience (sabr) is praised many times in the Qur'an: 'Indeed, Allah is with the patient' (al-Baqarah 2:153). Saving first instead of borrowing avoids debt and riba.

starter.a: Interest on loans, forbidden in Islam.

teach.heading: Set the goal
teach.note: Example: a £36 book set.

teach.heading: Make a plan
bullets: How much can I save each week?
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Goal £36, I save £5 a week. How long?

teach.heading: Speeding up
bullets: Earn a little (chores agreed with parents)
teach.note: Track on a chart.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Goal £30, save £4 a week. Weeks needed?

practice.model: Teacher divides and explains rounding up.

independent.q: Core: Saving plan sheet: choose a goal, price, weekly amount and timescale (pupil PDF).
independent.a: A complete plan with correct calculation.
independent.model: Teacher fills the plan for a £24 goal.

independent.q: Extend: Show how cutting one weekly want shortens your plan.
independent.a: A recalculation with the extra saving.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why saving is better than buying now with a riba loan.
independent.a: No extra cost, no debt, and it avoids what Islam forbids.

exit.q: Goal £20, save £5 a week. Weeks? A) 3 B) 4 C) 5
Big question: what helps you wait for a bigger reward?

lessons.unit: Summer 1: People around us
lessons.title: Ending a friendship kindly
lessons.bigQuestion: Is it ever OK for a friendship to end? How can it end without hurting someone more than needed?
objectives: To understand that friendships can change and how to end or step back from one kindly and safely
successCriteria: All: say why friendships change
Most: describe a kind way to step back
Some: know when a friendship is unsafe and needs an adult
lessons.smsc: Moral: kindness even when things change

keywords.def: becoming different over time
treating others as valuable
a friendship that makes you feel bad or unsafe
being gentle and caring

hook.text: Is it ever OK for a friendship to end? How can it end without hurting someone more than needed?
hook.a: Yes, friendships change; we can step back kindly, without gossip or cruelty.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'A man follows the religion of his close friend, so let each of you look at whom he befriends' (Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi, graded hasan).

starter.q: Give an assertive reply to a put-down.

teach.heading: Unhealthy friendships
teach.note: These need a trusted adult.

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: Which is a kind way to step back?
options: Spend more time with others and stay polite

practice.q: Write what you could say to a friend you see less often now.
practice.a: 'I've been busy with other things, but I still think you're great.'
practice.model: I do: 'I'm joining the Arabic club now so I'll see you less, but I'll still say salam.'

independent.q: Pupil PDF: three friendship scenarios; decide whether to work on it, step back, or tell an adult, and why.
independent.a: Three decisions with reasons.

independent.q: Extend: list three qualities you want in a friend at secondary school.
independent.a: Three qualities.

exit.q: A friendship that pressures you to do wrong is ...
exit.a: unhealthy: tell a trusted adult

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Is it ever OK for a friendship to end? How can it end without hurting someone more than needed?
exit.a: Yes, friendships change; we can step back kindly, without gossip or cruelty.

lessons.homework: Write a diary entry: what makes a good friend?
